citation.title: Average treatment effects in the presence of unknown interference

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 3.1, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] Consider a sample of $n$ units indexed by the set $\mathbf{U} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An experimenter intervenes on the world in ways that potentially affect the units. The intervention is described by a $n$-dimensional binary vector $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n) \in \{0, 1\}^n$. For short, we refer to $z_i$ as unit $i$'s treatment. Each unit has a function $y_i : \{0, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ denoting the observed outcome for the unit under a specific and potentially counterfactual intervention. In particular, $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ is the response of $i$ when the intervention is $\mathbf{z}$. We refer to the elements of the image of this function as potential outcomes. Let $\mathbf{z}_{-i} = (z_1, \ldots, z_{i-1}, z_{i+1}, \ldots, z_n)$ denote the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\mathbf{z}$. The potential outcome $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ can then be written as $y_i(z_i; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. Throughout the paper, we assume that the potential outcomes are well-defined. The experimenter sets $\mathbf{z}$ according to a random vector $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$. The probability distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ is the design of the experiment. The design is the sole source of randomness we will consider. Let $Y_i$ denote the observed outcome of unit $i$: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$. As above, $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ denotes $\mathbf{Z}$ without its $i$th element, so $Y_i = y_i(Z_i; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})$. [No interference: Section 3.2, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] It is conventional to assume that the potential outcomes are restricted so a unit's outcome is only affected by its own treatment. That is, for any two assignments $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$, if the treatment of a given unit is the same for both assignments, then the outcome for that unit is also the same. This no-interference assumption admits a definition of the treatment effect $\tau_i$ for unit $i$: $\tau_i = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$, where $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ is any element of $\{0, 1\}^{n-1}$. [Definitions 1 to 3: p. 677 (PDF p. 5)] DEFINITION 1. Under no interference, the average treatment effect (ATE) is the average unit-level treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i$. The assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect is $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i}) = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 2. An assignment-conditional average treatment effect is the average of the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effects under a given assignment: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 3. The expected average treatment effect (EATE) is the expected assignment-conditional average treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$, where the expectation is taken over the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ given by the experimental design. [Definition 4: p. 678 (PDF p. 6)] DEFINITION 4. The average distributional shift effect (ADSE) is the average difference between the conditional expected outcomes for the two treatment conditions: $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]\right)$. [Interference indicator: Section 4, p. 680 (PDF p. 8)] We say that unit $i$ interferes with unit $j$ if changing $i$'s treatment changes $j$'s outcome under at least one treatment assignment. We also say that a unit interferes with itself even if its own treatment does not affect its outcome. The indicator $I_{ij}$ denotes such interference: $I_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y_j(\mathbf{z}) \ne y_j(\mathbf{z}') \text{ for some } \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \{0, 1\}^n \text{ such that } \mathbf{z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}'_{-i}, \\ 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Definition 5 (Interference dependence): p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ where $d_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } I_{\ell i} I_{\ell j} = 1 \text{ for some } \ell \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ The sum $d_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ gives the number of interference dependencies for unit $i$. [Interference counts: p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $c_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{ij}$ and $C_p = \left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^p\right]^{1/p}$. We write $C_\infty$ for the limit of $C_p$ as $p \to \infty$, which is the maximum $c_i$ over $\mathbf{U}$. [Asymptotic regime: Section 5, pp. 681–682 (PDF pp. 9–10)] We consider an arbitrary sequence of samples indexed by their sample size. The samples are not assumed to be drawn from some larger population or otherwise randomly generated. All quantities describing the samples, such as the potential outcomes and experimental designs, have their own sequences also indexed by $n$. But we leave the indexing implicit as no confusion arises. [Definition 6: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) and Hájek (HÁ) estimators are $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i}$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i}{p_i}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - Z_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$, where $p_i = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ is the marginal treatment probability for unit $i$. [Assumption 1: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] We assume throughout the remainder of the paper that the experimental design and potential outcomes are sufficiently well behaved, as formalized in the following assumption. ASSUMPTION 1 (Regularity conditions). There exist constants $k < \infty$, $q \ge 2$ and $s \ge 1$ such that for all $i \in \mathbf{U}$ in the sequence of samples: A (Probabilistic assignment). $k^{-1} \le \Pr(Z_i = 1) \le 1 - k^{-1}$, B (Outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|Y_i|^q] \le k^q$, C (Potential outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})|^s] \le k^s$ for $z \in \{0, 1\}$. [Assumption 2: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] ASSUMPTION 2 (Restricted interference). $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = o(n)$. [Bernoulli design: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] We call this a Bernoulli randomization design, and it satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{z_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - z_i}$ for some set of assignment probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ bounded away from zero and one. [Complete randomization: p. 684 (PDF p. 12)] $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} \binom{n}{m}^{-1} & \text{if } \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i = m, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}$ where $m = \lfloor pn \rfloor$ for some fixed $p$ strictly between zero and one. We call the design complete randomization. [Paired randomization: p. 685 (PDF p. 13)] It is implicit that the sample size is even so that all units are paired. Let $\rho : \mathbf{U} \to \mathbf{U}$ describe a pairing so that $\rho(i) = j$ indicates that units $i$ and $j$ are paired. The pairing is symmetric, so the self-composition of $\rho$ is the identity function. The paired randomization design then satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} 2^{-n/2} & \text{if } z_i \ne z_{\rho(i)} \text{ for all } i \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Notation the paper uses without defining] The paper does not define $\mathcal{O}_p$, $o_p$, 'consistent' or 'root-$n$ consistent'. The proof of Lemma A5 (Supplement A, p. 4) uses $X_n - x_n = \mathcal{O}_p(a_n)$ in the sense that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are a constant $\kappa$ and an $N$ such that $\Pr(|X_n - x_n| \ge \kappa a_n) \le \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. 'Consistent for' an estimand means that the difference between the estimator and the estimand (both sequences in $n$) converges in probability to zero; 'root-$n$ consistent' means that this difference is $\mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5})$. Supplement A is the separate file 'Supplement A: Proofs' (41 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPA) and Supplement B is 'Supplement B: Simulation study' (21 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPB); their page numbers are their own printed page numbers, which equal their PDF page numbers. In the main article the printed page number is the PDF page number plus 672.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.1, the sentence 'inferences based on the estimator will be conservative also in large samples' (read with equation (1) and Definition 10), as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 689 (PDF p. 17), Section 6.1, the two sentences after the display of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})$, and equation (1). Definition 10: p. 691 (PDF p. 19). Propositions 8, 9 and 10: pp. 692–693 (PDF pp. 20–21)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [p. 689 (PDF p. 17), Section 6.1] $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i^2}{p_i^2} + \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i^2}{(1 - p_i)^2}$. The estimator is conservative under no interference, meaning that its expectation is greater than the true variance. On a normalized scale, the bias does not diminish asymptotically, so inferences based on the estimator will be conservative also in large samples. In particular, with a Bernoulli design under no interference, (1) $n\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})\right] \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} \tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}} \ge 0$, where $\tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}}$ is the mean square treatment effect [p. 690 (PDF p. 18)]. [What is refuted] The step from the variance property (expectation above the true variance, equation (1), asymptotic conservativeness in the sense of Definition 10) to conservative inference in large samples, read as coverage of at least the nominal level for the interval obtained by putting the variance estimate into Chebyshev's inequality. Equation (1), Definition 10 and Propositions 8, 9 and 10 are not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator] For each integer $n \ge 1$ let $Z_1, \ldots, Z_n$ be independent Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$), and let $y_1(\mathbf{z}) = z_1$ and $y_i(\mathbf{z}) = 0$ for $i \ge 2$, for every $\mathbf{z} \in \{0, 1\}^n$. Then: (a) Assumption 1 holds with $k = 2$ and every $q \ge 2$, $s \ge 1$ (all potential outcomes lie in $[0, 1]$); $I_{ij} = d_{ij} = \mathbb{1}[i = j]$, so there is no interference, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = d_{\mathrm{RMS}} = d_{\mathrm{MAX}} = \lambda_{\max} = 1$ and Assumption 2 holds. (b) $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = 1/n$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = 2Z_1/n$, $\mathrm{E}[\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}] = 1/n$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = 1/n^2$. (c) $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = 4Z_1/n^2$, so $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})] = 2/n^2 > \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})$, and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{MAX}} = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{SR}} = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}$. (d) $n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{-1}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})\right] = (4Z_1 - 1)/n \in \{-1/n,\ 3/n\}$. Hence for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every $n > 1/\varepsilon$, $\Pr\left(n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{-1}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})] \le -\varepsilon\right) = 0$, and the condition of Definition 10 holds for all four estimators. (e) $\tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}} = 1/n$ and $n[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})] - \tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}} = (4Z_1 - 2)/n \in \{-2/n,\ 2/n\}$, so equation (1) holds as convergence in probability of the difference to zero; the normalized expected bias is $n\left(\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})] - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})\right) = 1/n \to 0$. (f) The hypotheses of Proposition 8 hold: $\sigma_1^2 = 1$, $\sigma_i^2 = 0$ for $i \ge 2$, $\mathrm{SD}_{\sigma^2}^2 = (n - 1)/n^2 \to 0$ and $d_{\mathrm{RMS}}^{-1} d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = 1$. Those of Proposition 9A and Proposition 10A hold: $d_{\mathrm{MAX}}/(n^{0.5} d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5}) = \lambda_{\max}/(n^{0.5} d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5}) = n^{-0.5} \to 0$. (Part B of Propositions 9 and 10 does not apply: $\tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}} = 1/n$ is not $\Omega(1)$.) (g) For $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ let $I_n = \left[\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \sqrt{\hat V/\alpha},\ \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} + \sqrt{\hat V/\alpha}\right]$ with $\hat V = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})$. On $\{Z_1 = 0\}$, $I_n = [0, 0]$ does not contain $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = 1/n$; on $\{Z_1 = 1\}$, $(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}})^2 = 1/n^2 \le 4/(\alpha n^2) = \hat V/\alpha$. Hence $\Pr(\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} \in I_n) = \frac{1}{2}$ for every $n \ge 1$ and every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$; with $\alpha = \frac{1}{20}$ the nominal coverage is $\frac{19}{20}$. (h) $\Pr\left(\hat V < (1 - \eta)\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})\right) = \frac{1}{2}$ for every $\eta \in (0, 1)$, and $n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{-1}\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = 1/n \to 0$.

[Conventional variance estimator: Section 6.1, p. 689 (PDF p. 17)] The Horvitz–Thompson estimator of the variance of the Horvitz–Thompson point estimator under a Bernoulli design: $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i^2}{p_i^2} + \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i^2}{(1 - p_i)^2}$. [Mean square treatment effect: p. 690 (PDF p. 18)] $\tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{E}[\tau_i(\mathbf{Z}_{-i})]\right)^2$. [Definition 10: p. 691 (PDF p. 19)] A variance estimator $\hat V$ is said to be asymptotically conservative with respect to the variance of $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$ if $\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+}\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr\left(n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{-1}[\hat V - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})] \le -\varepsilon\right) = 0$. [Inflated estimators: pp. 691–693 (PDF pp. 19–21)] $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{AVG}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = d_{\mathrm{AVG}}\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})$ (p. 691); $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{MAX}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = d_{\mathrm{MAX}}\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})$, where $d_{\mathrm{MAX}}$ is the maximum of $d_i$ over $i \in \mathbf{U}$ (p. 692); let $\mathbf{D}$ be a matrix whose typical argument is $d_{ij}$, and let $\lambda_{\max}$ be the largest eigenvalue, or spectral radius, of this matrix (p. 692); $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{SR}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = \lambda_{\max}\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})$ (p. 693). [Quantities of Proposition 8: p. 692 (PDF p. 20)] $\mathrm{SD}_{\sigma^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\sigma_i^2 - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sigma_j^2\right]^2}$, $\sigma_i^2 = \mathrm{Var}\left(\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} - \frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$, $d_{\mathrm{RMS}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i^2}$. [Parts A of Propositions 9 and 10: pp. 692-693 (PDF pp. 20-21)] Proposition 9A: Assumption 1 holds with $q \ge 4$ and $d_{\mathrm{MAX}} = o(n^{0.5} d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5})$. Proposition 10A: Assumption 1 holds with $q \ge 4$ and $\lambda_{\max} = o(n^{0.5} d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5})$. Part B of each: Assumptions 1 and 2 hold with $q \ge 4$ and $\tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}} = \Omega(1)$. [The interval tested; the paper prints no interval formula] Section 6.3 (p. 693, PDF p. 21) says that experimenters use variance estimates to construct bounds on the tails of the sampling distribution of the point estimator, which in turn may be used to construct confidence intervals, and concludes (p. 694, PDF p. 22) that Chebyshev's inequality is an appropriate way to construct confidence intervals. The interval obtained by putting a variance estimate $\hat V$ into Chebyshev's inequality at level $\alpha$ is $I_n = \left[\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \sqrt{\hat V/\alpha},\ \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} + \sqrt{\hat V/\alpha}\right]$, with nominal coverage $1 - \alpha$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Every fact needed is exact for each fixed $n \ge 1$: the two-atom law of $(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}, \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}})$, namely $(0, 0)$ and $(2/n, 4/n^2)$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each; $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}} = 1/n$; $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) = 1/n^2$; $\Pr(n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{-1}[\hat V - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})] \le -\varepsilon) = 0$ whenever $n\varepsilon > 1$; $\mathrm{SD}_{\sigma^2}^2 = (n - 1)/n^2$; and $\Pr(\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} \in I_n) = \frac{1}{2}$. The limit statements (Definition 10, equation (1), the $o(\cdot)$ hypotheses of Propositions 8, 9A and 10A) follow from these at once.
canonical_claim.note: Rated an error, Minor. The same sequence of experiments is the counterexample for P009-E001. The paper prints no interval formula and no coverage theorem; the counterexample tests the natural plug-in construction and the inferential sentence on p. 689. Coverage is $\frac{1}{2}$ whichever of the four variance estimators is used, since they coincide here.

canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected sentence, replacing 'On a normalized scale, the bias does not diminish asymptotically, so inferences based on the estimator will be conservative also in large samples.'] Equation (1) gives a nonnegative one-sided scaled variance error; the scaled bias may vanish. This variance property alone does not establish conservative plug-in confidence intervals. Equation (1), Definition 10 and Propositions 8, 9 and 10 stand as printed. [Formal content of the corrected claim, with every hypothesis] Let, for each $n$, $T_n$ be a real random variable with $\mathrm{E}[T_n] = \theta_n$ and $V_n = \mathrm{Var}(T_n) \in (0, \infty)$, and let $\hat V_n \ge 0$ be a random variable on the same probability space. Fix $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and let $I_n = \left[T_n - \sqrt{\hat V_n/\alpha},\ T_n + \sqrt{\hat V_n/\alpha}\right]$. (i) For every $n$ and every $\eta \in (0, 1)$: $\Pr(\theta_n \notin I_n) \le \Pr\left(\hat V_n < (1 - \eta)V_n\right) + \frac{\alpha}{1 - \eta}$. Consequently, if $\Pr(\hat V_n < (1 - \eta)V_n) \to 0$ for every $\eta \in (0, 1)$, then $\liminf_{n \to \infty}\Pr(\theta_n \in I_n) \ge 1 - \alpha$. (ii) Let $(\delta_n)$ be a positive sequence (in the paper, $\delta_n = d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$). If for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr\left(n\delta_n^{-1}[\hat V_n - V_n] \le -\varepsilon\right) = 0$ (which the condition of Definition 10 implies, because this probability is nonincreasing in $\varepsilon$), and if $\liminf_{n \to \infty} n\delta_n^{-1}V_n > 0$, then $\Pr(\hat V_n < (1 - \eta)V_n) \to 0$ for every $\eta \in (0, 1)$. The finite step: if $n\delta_n^{-1}V_n \ge c > 0$, then $\{\hat V_n < (1 - \eta)V_n\} \subseteq \{n\delta_n^{-1}(\hat V_n - V_n) \le -\eta c\}$. (iii) Under a Bernoulli design and Assumption 1, $\mathrm{E}[\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}] = \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (Lemmas A1 and A8, Supplement A, pp. 3 and 7). Hence, for $T_n = \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\theta_n = \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ and $\hat V_n$ any nonnegative variance estimator that is asymptotically conservative in the sense of Definition 10: if $\liminf_{n \to \infty} n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{-1}\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) > 0$, then $\liminf_{n \to \infty}\Pr\left(\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} \in \left[\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \sqrt{\hat V_n/\alpha},\ \hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} + \sqrt{\hat V_n/\alpha}\right]\right) \ge 1 - \alpha$. Without the lower bound on the normalized variance the conclusion can fail (the counterexample target for this finding).

canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [p. 691 (PDF p. 19), Section 6.1] While any of the three terms of the limit in Proposition 7 can dominate the others asymptotically, $B_2$ will generally be the one we need to worry about. To see this, observe that $\tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}}$ is negligible on a normalized scale as long as the average interference dependence is not bounded asymptotically: $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} \to \infty$. The amount of direct interference dependence is given by $C_1$, so $B_1 = \mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{-1}C_1)$. The amount of indirect dependence is given by $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, so $B_2 = \mathcal{O}(1)$. [Counterexample, from the validator] For each integer $m \ge 2$ let $n = m^2$, partitioned into $m$ blocks of $m$ units; in each block label the units $0, 1, \ldots, m - 1$ (unit 0 the hub, unit 1 a distinguished leaf). All $Z_i$ are independent Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$). canonical_claim.statement: [Printed step] [Supplement A, p. 10] We have $T_i \le \reflectbox{c}_i \le \min(m, n - m)$, which, together with complete randomization, implies that $T_i$ is hyper-geometric according to: $\Pr(T_i = t) = \binom{m}{t}\binom{n - m}{\reflectbox{c}_i - t}\binom{n}{\reflectbox{c}_i}^{-1}$, $\Pr(T_i = t \mid Z_i = z) = z\binom{m - 1}{t}\binom{n - m}{\reflectbox{c}_i - t}\binom{n - 1}{\reflectbox{c}_i}^{-1} + (1 - z)\binom{m}{t}\binom{n - m - 1}{\reflectbox{c}_i - t}\binom{n - 1}{\reflectbox{c}_i}^{-1}$. [...] so we have: $\frac{\Pr(T_i = t \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(T_i = t)} - 1 = \frac{\reflectbox{c}_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)(n - \reflectbox{c}_i)}\left[\Pr(Z_i = z) - z\frac{t}{\reflectbox{c}_i} - (1 - z)\frac{\reflectbox{c}_i - t}{\reflectbox{c}_i}\right]$, where the last equality exploits that $n\Pr(Z_i = z) = zm + (1 - z)(n - m)$ under complete randomization. [What is refuted] The two printed laws and the printed identity for the ratio: $T_i$ counts treated units among the $\reflectbox{c}_i - 1$ units other than $i$ that interfere with $i$, so the number of draws is $\reflectbox{c}_i - 1$, not $\reflectbox{c}_i$. The inequality stated in Lemma A12 is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator] $n = 4$, $m = 2$ (complete randomization, six assignments of probability $\frac{1}{6}$), $i = 1$, $y_1(\mathbf{v}) = v_1 + v_2$ and $y_j(\mathbf{v}) = v_j$ for $j = 2, 3, 4$. Then $I_{11} = I_{21} = 1$ and $I_{31} = I_{41} = 0$, so $\reflectbox{c}_1 = 2 = \min(m, n - m)$ and $T_1 = Z_2$. For $t = 0, 1, 2$: the true $\Pr(T_1 = t)$ is $(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}, 0)$, the printed formula gives $(\frac{1}{6}, \frac{2}{3}, \frac{1}{6})$; the true $\Pr(T_1 = t \mid Z_1 = 1)$ is $(\frac{2}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, 0)$, the printed formula gives $(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}, 0)$; the true $\Pr(T_1 = t \mid Z_1 = 0)$ is $(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}, 0)$, the printed formula gives $(0, \frac{2}{3}, \frac{1}{3})$. At $t = 0$, $z = 1$ the true ratio is $\frac{2/3}{1/2} = \frac{4}{3}$, while the printed laws give $\frac{1/3}{1/6} = 2$. [Second instance] $n = 4$, $m = 2$, $y_j(\mathbf{v}) = v_j$ for all $j$ (no interference): $\reflectbox{c}_i = 1$ and $T_i = 0$ surely, but the printed formula gives $\Pr(T_i = 0) = \binom{2}{0}\binom{2}{1}\binom{4}{1}^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}$.
